prompt: The section's table of molar entropies lists the noble gases from He (4.0 g/mol) to Rn (222.0 g/mol). How does the standard molar entropy S° change down this list?

choices.text: It rises steadily as the molar mass rises
It falls as the molar mass rises
choices.why: The table shows the opposite: S° goes from 126.15 J/(mol·K) for He up to 176.2 J/(mol·K) for Rn. Heavier atoms have more entropy.

choices.text: It stays the same, since all are monatomic
choices.why: Being monatomic, they share the same kinds of motion, but their masses differ. S° climbs from 126.15 to 176.2 J/(mol·K) as the mass grows.

choices.text: It rises from He to Ar, then falls
choices.why: S° keeps rising all the way to Rn, at 176.2 J/(mol·K). There is no turning point in the table.

explanation: S° climbs from 126.15 J/(mol·K) for He through 154.84 J/(mol·K) for Ar to 176.2 J/(mol·K) for Rn. For atoms with the same kinds of motion, the heavier one has the higher entropy.

prompt: According to quantum theory, as quoted in the section, how does increasing the mass of a particle change the spacing between its energy states?

choices.text: The spacing gets smaller
The spacing gets larger
choices.why: A heavier particle has more closely spaced levels, not more widely spaced ones. That is why more of its states are reachable at a given temperature.

choices.text: The spacing does not depend on mass
choices.why: The section says that increasing the mass decreases the spacing between states. That is why heavier gases have more accessible states.

choices.text: Only the ground-state energy shifts
choices.why: The whole ladder of levels is squeezed together, not just the lowest one. Smaller spacings mean more states are reachable at a given temperature.

explanation: A heavier particle has its energy levels closer together. At a given temperature, more of them lie within reach of the thermal energy, so more states can be occupied.

prompt: At a given temperature, why do more closely spaced energy levels give a gas a higher entropy?

choices.text: More levels can be populated, giving more microstates
Each closely spaced level holds more energy
choices.why: The levels themselves don't hold more energy. What matters is that more of them are within reach, so the energy can be spread over more microstates.

choices.text: The temperature rises as the levels move closer
choices.why: The temperature is the same in this comparison. Closer levels raise S because more states can be occupied at that temperature.

choices.text: Fewer levels are occupied, so the gas is more ordered
choices.why: Closer spacing lets more levels be occupied, not fewer. More occupied levels means more microstates and a higher entropy.

explanation: Entropy grows with the number of microstates the particles can occupy. When the levels are closer together, more of them are reachable at the same temperature, so there are more ways to share out the energy.

prompt: The noble gases in the section's table are all monatomic. In which kind of motion are the closely spaced energy levels that give the heavier atoms more entropy?

choices.text: Translation of the atom through space
Vibration of the atom's bonds
choices.why: A single atom has no bonds, so it cannot vibrate. Its mass enters through its translational levels, which crowd closer together for heavier atoms.

choices.text: Rotation of the atom about an axis
choices.why: A single atom has no rotational levels to fill in the way a molecule does. The mass dependence comes from its translational levels.

choices.text: Excitation of electrons to higher shells
choices.why: The electronic excited states of the noble gases lie far above the thermal energy at room temperature. The mass effect comes through the closely spaced translational levels.

explanation: A monatomic gas can only move its atoms through space, and the translational levels of a heavier atom lie closer together. That is why S° rises from He to Rn.

prompt: CO2 has S° = 213.8 J/(mol·K) and CH4 has S° = 186.3 J/(mol·K). According to the section, what mainly gives CO2 the higher standard entropy?

choices.text: Its greater mass and moment of inertia
Its larger number of atoms
choices.why: CO2 has 3 atoms and CH4 has 5, so counting atoms favours methane. CO2 wins mainly through its greater mass (44 vs 16 g/mol) and moment of inertia.

choices.text: Its triplet electronic ground state
choices.why: That is the reason O2 beats N2, not the reason CO2 beats CH4. CO2's advantage comes mainly from its greater mass and moment of inertia.

choices.text: Its vibrations, which are fully excited at 298 K
choices.why: Molecular vibrations are only slightly excited at room temperature. CO2's advantage comes mainly from its greater mass and moment of inertia.

explanation: A CO2 molecule (44 g/mol) is much heavier than a CH4 molecule (16 g/mol) and has a larger moment of inertia, so its translational and rotational levels lie closer together. That outweighs methane's extra atoms.

prompt: A CH4 molecule has more atoms and more vibrational modes than a CO2 molecule, yet its S° is lower. Why do methane's extra vibrations add so little entropy at 298 K?

choices.text: They are hardly excited at room temperature
Vibrations never add anything to the entropy
choices.why: Vibrations do add entropy once they are excited. Methane's are simply hardly excited at 298 K.

choices.text: Methane is linear, so its atoms cannot vibrate
choices.why: Methane is tetrahedral, not linear, and every molecule with two or more atoms can vibrate. Its vibrations just need more energy than is available at 298 K.

choices.text: Its vibrations cancel its rotations
choices.why: Different kinds of motion add to the entropy; they never cancel. Methane's vibrations add little only because they are hardly excited at 298 K.

explanation: Methane's vibrational levels are widely spaced compared with k_B T at 298 K, so almost every molecule sits in its vibrational ground state. Modes that are not excited add almost no microstates, so CO2's greater mass wins.

prompt: O2 has a higher standard entropy than N2. According to the section, what mainly causes the difference?

choices.text: O2's triplet electronic ground state
O2's larger molar mass, 32 vs 28 g/mol
choices.why: The small difference in mass explains only a small part of the gap. Most of it comes from O2's threefold-degenerate (triplet) electronic ground state.

choices.text: O2 has more vibrational modes than N2
choices.why: Both are diatomic, so each has exactly one vibration. The main cause is O2's threefold-degenerate electronic ground state.

choices.text: O2 is bent, so it can rotate in more ways
choices.why: O2, like N2, is a linear diatomic molecule. Its extra entropy comes mainly from its threefold-degenerate electronic ground state.

explanation: O2's ground electronic state is a triplet: three states with the same energy, which adds R ln 3 = 9.1 J/(mol·K) to its molar entropy. That is most of the gap between O2 and N2; the slightly greater mass of O2 supplies the rest.

prompt: According to the section, why does a molecule with more atoms generally have a higher entropy?

choices.text: It has more degrees of freedom
Its atoms are held more rigidly in place
choices.why: Rigid atoms would mean fewer ways to store energy, which lowers entropy. More atoms give more rotations and vibrations to take up energy.

choices.text: It has fewer ways to arrange its energy
choices.why: More atoms give more ways, not fewer: more rotational and vibrational modes. More ways to store energy means more microstates and a higher S.

choices.text: Its molar mass is always lower
choices.why: Adding atoms makes a molecule heavier, not lighter. The section's reason is the extra degrees of freedom that can take up energy.

explanation: Each extra atom adds ways for the molecule to rotate and vibrate. More degrees of freedom mean more accessible quantum states and more microstates, so a higher entropy, though only the modes that are excited at room temperature count much.

prompt: Ethane, C2H6, is heavier than methane, CH4, and has more atoms. Based on the section, how should their standard molar entropies as gases compare?

choices.text: S° of C2H6 is higher
S° of CH4 is higher
choices.why: Both of the section's trends point the other way: C2H6 is heavier and has more atoms. Its S° is the higher one.

choices.text: They are equal, as both are hydrocarbons
choices.why: Belonging to the same family does not fix the entropy. Ethane's greater mass and extra atoms give it more microstates.

choices.text: It can't be predicted without a calculation
choices.why: Here both trends agree, so the prediction is safe: more mass and more atoms both raise S°. Only when the trends conflict, as for CH4 and CO2, is it hard to call.

explanation: More mass gives more closely spaced levels, and more atoms give more degrees of freedom. Both favour ethane, and indeed S° is roughly 230 J/(mol·K) for C2H6(g) against 186.3 J/(mol·K) for CH4(g).

prompt: F2 and Cl2 are both diatomic molecules with the same kinds of motion, but Cl2 is almost twice as heavy (71 vs 38 g/mol). Which should have the higher S°, and why?

choices.text: Cl2, since its levels lie closer together
F2, because lighter molecules move faster
choices.why: Speed is not what counts; the number of accessible states is. Heavier Cl2 has more closely spaced levels, so more microstates.

choices.text: Neither, since the structures are the same
choices.why: The same structure only means the same kinds of motion. The heavier molecule has those levels closer together, so Cl2 has the higher S°.

choices.text: F2, because fluorine is more electronegative
choices.why: Electronegativity doesn't enter. With the same structure, the heavier molecule, Cl2, has more closely spaced levels and the higher S°.

explanation: With the same structure, mass decides: the levels of Cl2 lie closer together, so more of them are occupied at 298 K. Indeed S° is about 223 J/(mol·K) for Cl2 against about 203 J/(mol·K) for F2.

prompt: Ne (20.2 g/mol) and HF (20.0 g/mol) have almost the same mass. Which should have the higher standard entropy as a gas, and why?

choices.text: HF, since a molecule can also rotate
Ne, since it is slightly heavier
choices.why: A 1% difference in mass changes S° very little. HF's rotations add many more accessible states, so HF has the higher S°.

choices.text: They are equal, since their masses match
choices.why: Equal mass gives similar translational entropy, but HF also has rotational states. That extra kind of motion gives HF the higher S°.

choices.text: Ne, since atoms are less ordered than molecules
choices.why: An atom has fewer ways to hold energy than a molecule, not more. HF's extra rotational states raise its S° above neon's.

explanation: With the mass nearly the same, structure decides. HF can rotate as well as move through space, which adds accessible quantum states: S° is about 174 J/(mol·K) for HF(g) against 146.33 J/(mol·K) for Ne.

prompt: Why should the molecular mass and molecular structure of a gas affect its standard entropy at all?

choices.text: They change how many microstates are available
They change the temperature the gas settles at
choices.why: S° is compared at the same temperature for every gas. Mass and structure matter because they change the number of accessible microstates.

choices.text: They change the pressure of the gas
choices.why: S° is always taken at the same standard pressure, 1 bar. Mass and structure act through the number of microstates the molecules can occupy.

choices.text: They set the gas's enthalpy of formation
choices.why: Enthalpy of formation is a different quantity. Entropy depends on the number of microstates, which mass and structure change.

explanation: Entropy is tied to the number of microstates a collection of particles can occupy. Mass changes the spacing of the energy levels, and structure changes how many kinds of motion there are; both change that number.

prompt: The section's table gives S° = 154.84 J/(mol·K) for Ar and S° = 169.68 J/(mol·K) for Xe. By how much does S° rise from Ar to Xe, in J/(mol·K)? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: S°(Xe) − S°(Ar) = 169.68 − 154.84 = 14.84 J/(mol·K). Xenon (131.3 g/mol) is over three times as heavy as argon (39.9 g/mol), and its more closely spaced translational levels give it more entropy.

prompt: Rn (222.0 g/mol) is about 55 times as heavy as He (4.0 g/mol). The section's table gives S° = 176.2 J/(mol·K) for Rn and S° = 126.15 J/(mol·K) for He. What is the ratio of the S° of Rn to the S° of He? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 176.2 ÷ 126.15 = 1.397, so a 55-fold increase in mass raises S° by only about 40%. Entropy rises with mass, but far more slowly than in proportion to it.

prompt: The standard molar entropies are S° = 205.15 J/(mol·K) for O2 and S° = 191.61 J/(mol·K) for N2. By how much does S° of O2 exceed that of N2, in J/(mol·K)? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 205.15 − 191.61 = 13.54 J/(mol·K). About 9.1 J/(mol·K) of this, R ln 3, comes from the threefold-degenerate (triplet) ground state of O2; its slightly greater mass supplies the rest.
